chapter.title: A photo, not a film

cards.body: At one minute to midnight on 31 December, someone walks up to the house and takes a single photo. **A balance sheet is that photo.** It shows the house, the mortgage and the unpaid bills exactly as they stood on that one day, and nothing about the year that led there.
cards.simpler: It is one minute to midnight on 31 December. Someone walks up to a house and takes one photo. **A balance sheet is that photo.** It shows the house, the home loan and the unpaid bills exactly as they stood on that one day. It says nothing about the year that led up to it. It cannot show how the people inside got there, only where things sat when the camera clicked.

cards.prompt: Your friend Lena shows you a photo of her flat taken on 31 March. From the photo alone, can you tell what she earned in March?

options.text: Yes. A nicer flat means a bigger salary.
No. The photo shows what is there on one day, not what came in during the month.
Yes, if you can see the mortgage letter on the table.

whyNot.a: That's reading wealth as income: a flat can be inherited, borrowed against, or bought years ago. The photo shows what she has, not what she earned.
whyNot.c: That's what she owes, not what she earned: a mortgage letter is part of the photo, and still says nothing about March's pay.

cards.reteach: A photo freezes one moment. It can show a full fridge, but not how many shopping trips filled it. A balance sheet works the same way: one day, what is there, no record of the flow in or out.

cards.title: Find the date
cards.body:
Look at the top of any balance sheet. It says *as at* and then one date, often the last day of a financial year. **That one date is the whole claim.** Every number below it is true for that day only.

Compare the income statement, the second main report. Its heading says *for the year ended*, a stretch of time. That is the film: sales coming in, wages going out, 12 months of motion.

The photo has no 'from' and no 'to'. One day. If you remember nothing else from this page, remember the two words *as at*.
cards.simpler: Look at the top of any balance sheet. It says *as at* and then one date. Often that date is the last day of a financial year. **That one date is the whole claim.** Every number below it is true for that day only. The income statement is the other main report. Its heading says *for the year ended*, which is a stretch of time, like a film. The balance sheet has no 'from' and no 'to'. Just one day. Remember the words *as at*.

cards.title: Maya's oven
cards.body:
Maya runs a bakery. Her balance sheet as at 31 December shows cash 12,000, an oven worth 8,000 and a bank loan of 15,000. Nowhere does it say she sold 400 loaves a week, or that August was dreadful. **The oven does not know whether it was a good year.**

On 2 January she pays 10,000 off the loan. A photo taken that evening shows cash 2,000 and a loan of 5,000. Same bakery, two days later, and the picture looks like a different business.
cards.simpler: Maya runs a bakery. Her balance sheet as at 31 December shows cash of 12,000, an oven worth 8,000 and a bank loan of 15,000. It does not say she sold 400 loaves a week. It does not say August was dreadful. **The oven does not know whether it was a good year.** On 2 January she pays 10,000 off the loan. A photo taken that evening shows cash of 2,000 and a loan of 5,000. Same bakery, two days later, and it looks like a different business.

cards.prompt: Tomasz's bike shop has a balance sheet as at 30 June showing cash of 5,000. On 1 July a customer pays him 20,000 for a bulk order. What happens to the 30 June sheet?

options.text: It gets updated to show cash of 25,000, since the money was earned on that order.
It stays at 5,000. The 20,000 would show on a sheet dated 1 July or later.
The 20,000 is added as income on the 30 June sheet.

whyNot.a: That's mixing two dates: the photo was taken on 30 June, and nothing that happened in July can appear in it.
whyNot.c: That's the income statement's job, not the balance sheet's: a balance sheet has no income line at all, only what is there on the day.

cards.reteach: Think of the date as the shutter click. Whatever was in the till at that second is on the sheet. Money that arrives the next morning belongs to the next photo, not this one.

cards.title: Two photos, one story
cards.body:
You'd think one photo was enough. It is the second photo that tells you anything. Most published balance sheets print two columns side by side: this year-end and the one before. **Two dates a year apart show the movement.** Cash up, loan down, more unpaid customer bills: you cannot see the film, but you can see where the furniture moved.

One quiet catch. A company picks its own year-end, and some pick a day when stock is low and cash is high. The photo is honest. The house was just tidied before the camera came out.
cards.simpler: You might think one photo is enough. It is the second photo that tells you something. Most published balance sheets print two columns side by side: this year-end and last year-end. **Two dates a year apart show the movement.** Cash up, loan down, more unpaid customer bills. You cannot see the film, but you can see where the furniture moved. One quiet catch. A company picks its own year-end. Some pick a day when stock is low and cash is high. The photo is honest. The house was just tidied before the camera came out.

cards.body: Priya opens a balance sheet dated 31 March, sees 'Cash 40,000', and tells her brother the company makes 40,000 a year. Her brother asks where it says 'a year'. It doesn't. **The tell is the heading**: if it reads *as at*, nothing on the page is earnings, only what the company held on that day.
cards.simpler: Priya opens a balance sheet dated 31 March. She sees 'Cash 40,000' and tells her brother the company makes 40,000 a year. Her brother asks where the page says 'a year'. It does not. **The tell is the heading.** If it reads *as at*, nothing on the page is earnings. It only shows what the company held on that one day. Cash in the drawer is not the same as money made over a year.

cards.prompt: You want to know how much a company earned over the last 12 months. Which page do you open?

options.text: The balance sheet, because it lists cash and cash is what you earn.
The income statement, the one headed 'for the year ended'.
Either one, as long as it is dated 31 December.

whyNot.a: That's what the company holds on one day, not what it earned: cash can come from a loan or an investor just as easily as from sales.
whyNot.c: That's the date, not the type of report: the balance sheet is dated to a day, and the income statement covers the year before that day. Only the second one measures earnings.

cards.reteach: Earning takes time, and the balance sheet has no time in it. It is one frame. To see what came in over a year, you need the report that covers a year: the income statement.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A balance sheet is **a photo of a company on one date**, which you find next to the words 'as at' at the top. It shows what was there that day, never what was earned, and the second column, last year's photo, is where the story starts.

Tomorrow: assets are listed in strict order, and that order means speed to cash.
cards.simpler: A balance sheet is **a photo of a company on one date**. You find that date next to the words 'as at' at the top. It shows what was there on that day. It never shows what was earned. The second column is last year's photo, and that is where the story starts, because now you can see what moved. Tomorrow we look at assets. They are listed in a strict order, and that order tells you how fast each one turns into cash.

cards.body: Search online for any listed company's latest annual report. Find the balance sheet, read the heading, and say the date out loud. Then find the second column and say that date too.
cards.simpler: Search online for any listed company's latest annual report. A listed company is one whose shares are traded on a stock exchange, so its reports are public. Find the balance sheet inside the report. Read the heading and say the date out loud. Then find the second column, which is last year's figures, and say that date too. **Two dates, said out loud**, is the whole exercise. It takes about two minutes.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now say which single day a balance sheet describes and explain why it cannot tell you what the company earned.
